claims.text: RHEAs have superior mechanical strength at high temperatures.
RHEAs are promising materials for advanced nuclear-reactor applications.
The initial refractory-element/Cu mixture is mechanically mixed.
A large positive heat of mixing between refractory elements and Cu thermodynamically predisposes the mixture to phase separation.
Enhanced Monte Carlo or molecular dynamics with metadynamics can map free-energy landscapes and identify suitable rapid thermal-processing windows for refractory/Cu mixtures.
Free-energy-sampling-guided rapid heating and quenching can overcome the refractory/Cu mixing barrier.
High-temperature transient kinetics can temporarily suppress phase separation in refractory/Cu mixtures.
Rapid quenching from transient reaction conditions can stabilize a metastable refractory/Cu composite microstructure.
The resulting microstructure will be finely and homogeneously intermixed while integrating refractory phases with copper.
There are processing windows in which reaction kinetics temporarily dominate unfavorable refractory/Cu mixing thermodynamics.
A rapid thermal cycle can promote a fast in-situ reaction between refractory components and copper.
Rapid thermal processing can bypass the positive mixing enthalpy kinetically and prevent phase segregation.
The proposed method can produce a large-scale RHEA–Cu composite with a stable microstructure.
The resulting RHEA–Cu composite will meet high-temperature performance criteria for nuclear-reactor components.
The resulting RHEA–Cu composite will meet irradiation-resistance criteria for nuclear-reactor components.
Traditional melting, sintering, and additive-manufacturing routes produce phase-separated and unstable refractory/Cu microstructures because they do not exploit transient kinetic windows.
The method requires precise control of transient thermal profiles and composition-specific process optimization.
The magnitude of microstructure stabilization and scalability under reactor-relevant conditions remains experimentally unvalidated.
